facts.fact: AWS Organizations is the tenancy hierarchy: an organization has one administrative root, one management account, zero or more member accounts and nested organizational units (OUs) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_getting-started_concepts.html)

An SCP attached to the AWS Organizations root applies to all OUs and member accounts but not to the management account (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_getting-started_concepts.html)

A declarative policy attached to the AWS Organizations root also applies to the management account, unlike an SCP (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_getting-started_concepts.html)

The AWS account is the unit of quota, billing and Region-scoped resources; AgentCore and Bedrock quotas are per account per Region unless noted (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)

A client engagement normally gets one or more dedicated AWS workload accounts inside the client's AWS organization, because quotas are per account per Region (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)

Bedrock model access is on by default in commercial Regions with no access-request step; most models activate on first invocation if the caller has aws-marketplace:Subscribe, aws-marketplace:Unsubscribe and aws-marketplace:ViewSubscriptions plus a valid payment method (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)
Activating a Bedrock model on first invocation requires the caller to have `aws-marketplace:Subscribe` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)
Activating a Bedrock model on first invocation requires the caller to have `aws-marketplace:Unsubscribe` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)

facts.source: Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock
facts.target: Amazon Bedrock First Time Use (FTU) form
facts.fact: Anthropic models on Bedrock older than Claude Opus 4.7 need a one-time First Time Use (FTU) form, submitted in the console or with the PutUseCaseForModelAccess API, once per account or once at the organization's management account, and member accounts inherit it (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)

Claude Opus 4.7 is available on Amazon Bedrock and is the version from which Anthropic models no longer need the First Time Use form (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)

facts.target: Amazon Bedrock First Time Use (FTU) form
facts.fact: The `PutUseCaseForModelAccess` API submits the Bedrock Anthropic First Time Use form programmatically (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)
The Anthropic First Time Use form isn't required for Anthropic models called through the `bedrock-mantle` endpoint (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)

The first Bedrock model invocation sets up the AWS Marketplace subscription in the background; calls may succeed for up to 15 minutes and then fail with `AccessDeniedException` if a prerequisite is missing, and after the fix you should allow up to 2 minutes (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)
`GetFoundationModelAvailability` checks a Bedrock model's subscription status through the `agreementAvailability` field (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)

Some Bedrock models need additional account-level access that activation doesn't grant; access is decided per account, so accounts in the same organization can differ, and AWS Sales must be contacted if `AccessDeniedException` persists (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)

Invoking a third-party Bedrock model counts as accepting its EULA, so organizations that must review a EULA should first block model access with SCPs or IAM, review the third-party EULA, then allow access (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)

Programmatic Bedrock model activation runs `aws bedrock list-foundation-model-agreement-offers --model-id <id>` then `aws bedrock create-foundation-model-agreement --model-id <id> --offer-token <token>`; `offerType` `ALL` includes private offers (https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/bedrock-resolve-marketplace-permission ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)

Third-party Bedrock model private offers should be accepted from the management account or a delegated administrator; otherwise the offer can't be distributed through AWS Marketplace and member accounts are billed public rates until AWS License Manager grants are created (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/managed-entitlements-subscribing.html)

Distributing an accepted Bedrock private offer to member accounts depends on AWS License Manager grants; until they exist, member accounts pay public rates (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/managed-entitlements-subscribing.html)

Day-one asks for an engineer joining an AWS client: an IAM Identity Center user and permission set in the target workload account(s); the target Region(s) and any Region-deny SCP; confirmation that Bedrock model prerequisites are done (Marketplace permissions, Anthropic FTU, payment method); quota levels for the chosen models; VPC, subnet and security group IDs if VPC mode is required; and the corporate IdP discovery URL and client IDs for AgentCore JWT inbound auth (secondary: synthesis of the sources in this note) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/howtosessionduration.html)

An engineer joining an AWS client should ask for an IAM Identity Center user and permission set in the target workload account(s) (secondary: synthesis of the sources in this note) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/howtosessionduration.html)
Amazon Quick was renamed AWS Quick in a What's New post dated 2026-11-09; customers don't need to take any action (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/11/amazon-quick-aws-quick/)

The product that launched as Amazon Quick Suite was renamed twice, first to Amazon Quick and then to AWS Quick (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/11/amazon-quick-aws-quick/ ; https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/10/amazon-quick-suite-agentic-ai-powered-workspace/)

facts.fact: AWS Quick has a 30-day free trial covering up to 25 users per account (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/build-ai-powered-employee-onboarding-agents-with-amazon-quick/)
IAM Identity Center is the AWS human SSO layer and federates an external IdP over SAML (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/gs-okta.html)
IAM Identity Center provisions users and groups over SCIM 2.0 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/gs-okta.html)
Okta SCIM provisioning to IAM Identity Center supports create, update, deactivate, group push and import (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/gs-okta.html)

Microsoft Entra ID SCIM provisioning to IAM Identity Center doesn't unpack nested groups: only direct members of assigned groups are provisioned (dynamic groups do work), and attribute removals in Entra ID don't sync (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/idp-microsoft-entra.html)
Microsoft Entra ID can provision users and groups to IAM Identity Center over SCIM (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/idp-microsoft-entra.html)

IAM Identity Center permission-set session duration defaults to 1 hour and can be set up to 12 hours; Identity Center creates an IAM role per permission set in each assigned account, with a 12-hour maximum session (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/howtosessionduration.html)
Permission sets are part of IAM Identity Center and are provisioned as an IAM role in each assigned account (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/howtosessionduration.html)

The AWS access portal session is a separate, global IAM Identity Center setting from 15 minutes to 90 days (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/define-a-custom-session-duration-and-terminate-active-sessions-in-iam-identity-center/)

facts.source: IAM Identity Center trusted identity propagation
facts.fact: IAM Identity Center trusted identity propagation carries the end-user identity to AWS services: an external OIDC IdP is registered as a trusted token issuer and a customer managed application authorizes the token exchange for a specific `aud` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/trustedidentitypropagation-overview.html)

facts.source: IAM Identity Center trusted identity propagation
facts.fact: Trusted identity propagation accepts tokens from an external OIDC IdP registered as a trusted token issuer (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/trustedidentitypropagation-overview.html)

facts.target: IAM Identity Center trusted identity propagation
facts.fact: Services such as Quick and Amazon Q Business use trusted identity propagation to authorize by user or group and may log the user in CloudTrail (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/configuring-amazon-q-business-with-aws-iam-identity-center-trusted-identity-propagation/)

STS role sessions run from 900 seconds to the role's maximum, which is configurable from 1 to 12 hours, and `DurationSeconds` defaults to 3600 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/sts/assume-role-with-saml.html)

STS role chaining caps the session at 1 hour and the limit can't be raised; `AssumeRole` fails if `DurationSeconds` is over 3600 when chaining, which matters for long-running agent jobs (https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/iam-role-chaining-limit)

An STS call can pass one inline session policy and up to 10 managed policy ARNs, with plaintext of at most 2,048 characters, and the effective permissions are the intersection with the role's policies (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/sts/assume-role-with-saml.html)

GitHub Actions keyless federation uses an IAM OIDC provider for `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com` with client ID `sts.amazonaws.com`, and a role trust policy with `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` and conditions on `token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud` and `token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityagent/latest/userguide/sample-cicd-github.html)
The AWS role trusted by GitHub Actions must allow `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` in its trust policy (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityagent/latest/userguide/sample-cicd-github.html)

IAM rejects, on create or update, GitHub OIDC trust policies that lack a `token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub` (or `job_workflow_ref`) condition or whose value is only wildcards; when `sub` names a GitHub environment, also restrict `ref` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_create_for-idp_oidc.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/terraform-aws-provider-best-practices/security.html)

facts.source: Google Cloud workload identity federation to AWS
facts.fact: Google Cloud workloads can assume AWS roles without creating an IAM OIDC provider by using `"Principal": {"Federated": "accounts.google.com"}` with `StringEquals` on `accounts.google.com:aud` (maps to the token's `azp`), `accounts.google.com:oaud` (maps to `aud`) and `accounts.google.com:sub` (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/access-aws-using-a-google-cloud-platform-native-workload-identity/)

The IAM OIDC provider and the role must be in the same account; a wrong provider ARN in `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` returns `InvalidIdentityToken ... No OpenIDConnect provider found in your account` (https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/iam-oidc-idp-federation)

IAM Roles Anywhere gives non-AWS workloads temporary credentials for X.509 certificates, using a trust anchor (your CA or AWS Private CA), roles that trust the Roles Anywhere service, and profiles that scope down permissions (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/rolesanywhere/latest/console/hp-roles-anywhere.html)
An IAM Roles Anywhere trust anchor can be your own CA or AWS Private CA (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/rolesanywhere/latest/console/hp-roles-anywhere.html)

IAM outbound identity federation, announced 2025-11-19, lets AWS workloads authenticate to other clouds and SaaS without stored secrets; it is enabled per account under IAM Account settings and has no extra cost (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/simplify-access-to-external-services-using-aws-iam-outbound-identity-federation/)

A principal with `sts:GetWebIdentityToken` gets an AWS-signed JWT that the external service verifies against a JWKS endpoint (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/simplify-access-to-external-services-using-aws-iam-outbound-identity-federation/)
IAM outbound identity federation token lifetime is 60 to 3600 seconds, default 300 (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/simplify-access-to-external-services-using-aws-iam-outbound-identity-federation/)

facts.fact: IAM outbound identity federation can be restricted with the condition keys `sts:IdentityTokenAudience`, `sts:DurationSeconds` and `sts:SigningAlgorithm` (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/simplify-cross-partition-access-with-aws-iam-outbound-identity-federation/)

IAM outbound federation tokens can't be used for OIDC federation back into AWS through `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/simplify-cross-partition-access-with-aws-iam-outbound-identity-federation/)
IAM outbound web identity federation is enabled with the `EnableOutboundWebIdentityFederation` API (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_providers_outbound_getting_started.html)

The PowerShell cmdlet `Enable-IAMOutboundWebIdentityFederation` enables IAM outbound web identity federation (http://docs.aws.amazon.com/powershell/v4/reference/index.html?page=Enable-IAMOutboundWebIdentityFederation.html&tocid=Enable-IAMOutboundWebIdentityFederation)
Amazon Bedrock API keys exist for tools that only accept a bearer token (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/accelerate-ai-development-with-amazon-bedrock-api-keys/)

Short-term Bedrock API keys inherit the generating principal's IAM permissions and last up to 12 hours or the session length, whichever is shorter; long-term keys have an expiry from 1 day to never (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/accelerate-ai-development-with-amazon-bedrock-api-keys/)

A long-term Bedrock API key creates an IAM user with the `AmazonBedrockLimitedAccess` managed policy (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/accelerate-ai-development-with-amazon-bedrock-api-keys/)

AWS recommends STS credentials over Bedrock API keys: use short-term keys only when SigV4 isn't possible, and use SCPs to deny creating or using keys if they aren't needed (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/securing-amazon-bedrock-api-keys-best-practices-for-implementation-and-management/)

SigV4 with STS credentials is the AWS-recommended alternative to Bedrock API keys; short-term keys are for when SigV4 isn't possible (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/securing-amazon-bedrock-api-keys-best-practices-for-implementation-and-management/)

`aws-bedrock-token-generator` (Python) and `@aws/bedrock-token-generator` (JS) mint short-term Bedrock API keys from existing credentials (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/api-keys-generate.html)
The JS package `@aws/bedrock-token-generator` mints short-term Bedrock API keys from existing credentials (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/api-keys-generate.html)
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity is AWS's agent identity offering, built for AI agents and automated workloads (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/identity.html)

Each AgentCore agent identity is a workload identity with agent-specific attributes, kept in a workload identity directory (`workload-identity-directory/default`) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/identity.html)

AgentCore Runtime creates a workload identity for each deployed agent automatically (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/propagate-user-authorization-context-in-ai-agents-with-amazon-bedrock-agentcore/)

The AgentCore token vault stores agent OAuth client credentials, users' third-party OAuth tokens (after consent) and API keys, refreshes expired tokens, and re-prompts the user when needed (https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/faqs/)
The token vault is AgentCore Identity's store for agent OAuth tokens and API keys (https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/faqs/)

For production, agent code calls `GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT`: AgentCore validates the end user's IdP JWT signature and expiry and keys stored credentials to `iss` and `sub` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/get-workload-access-token.html)
`GetWorkloadAccessTokenForUserId` takes a caller-supplied user ID string with no IdP verification (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/get-workload-access-token.html)

AgentCore Identity also exposes `GetWorkloadAccessToken` for workload access tokens, alongside the ForJWT and ForUserId variants (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/get-workload-access-token.html)

AgentCore outbound OAuth supports two flows: `M2M` (client credentials) and `USER_FEDERATION` (three-legged, authorization code) (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/secure-ai-agents-with-amazon-bedrock-agentcore-identity-on-amazon-ecs/)

Each AgentCore OAuth2 credential provider gets a unique callback URL `https://bedrock-agentcore.<region>.amazonaws.com/identities/oauth2/callback/<uuid>`, returned by `CreateOauth2CredentialProvider`, which you register with the IdP afterwards (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/identity-idp-notion.html)
On-Behalf-Of (OBO) token exchange was added to AgentCore Identity in the April 2026 release notes (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

Since July 2026 AgentCore Identity supports Private Key JWT client authentication, with the key held in AWS KMS and RS256, PS256 or ES256 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)
AgentCore Identity Private Key JWT client authentication keeps the key in AWS KMS (July 2026) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)
Since July 2026 AgentCore Identity can reference existing AWS Secrets Manager secrets (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)
A Consent Portal was added to AgentCore Identity in September 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)
Since April 2026 AgentCore Identity supports VPC egress to private IdPs (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

An AgentCore Runtime or Gateway uses either SigV4 (IAM) or OAuth (JWT) inbound auth, not both, chosen at creation; JWT invocation is a plain HTTPS request with `Authorization: Bearer` that AWS SDKs don't manage (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/resource-based-policies.html ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/industries/automate-customer-complaint-classification-with-ai-agents-on-aws/)

facts.fact: AgentCore Runtime calls signed with IAM SigV4 propagate the user identity through the `X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-User-Id` header (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/industries/automate-customer-complaint-classification-with-ai-agents-on-aws/)

AgentCore Gateway inbound auth has four types: `CUSTOM_JWT` (OIDC or RFC 8414 discovery URL plus allowed clients), IAM, `AUTHENTICATE_ONLY` (SigV4 verified, no authorization) and `NONE` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-inbound-auth.html)

With IAM inbound auth, an AgentCore Gateway caller needs `bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway` scoped to the gateway ARN (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-inbound-auth.html)

With `AUTHENTICATE_ONLY` or `NONE` inbound auth the AgentCore Gateway enforces nothing, so a policy engine, an interceptor Lambda or the target must authorize; AWS says not to use `NONE` in production without those controls (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-inbound-auth.html)

JWT inbound auth on AgentCore Gateway logs the token's subject in CloudTrail, so AWS advises against PII in `sub` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-inbound-auth.html)

`GATEWAY_IAM_ROLE` (SigV4 with the gateway service role) is the AgentCore Gateway outbound credential type for Lambda, API Gateway, Smithy and connector targets; MCP server and OpenAPI targets also need `iamCredentialProvider.service` (for example `bedrock-agentcore`, `execute-api`, `lambda`) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-building-adding-targets-authorization.html)

Besides `GATEWAY_IAM_ROLE`, AgentCore Gateway outbound credential types are OAuth (via an AgentCore Identity credential provider), API key and none (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-outbound-auth.html)

Gateway-to-runtime auth types must match: an IAM runtime needs IAM (SigV4) or Caller IAM credentials, a JWT runtime needs OAuth (JWT) or Token passthrough, and a mismatch returns "Authorization method mismatch" (https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/bedrock-resolve-authorization-method)

MFA is mandatory for the management account root user; it must be registered at first sign-in or within a 14-day grace period (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/root-user-best-practices.html)

Centralized root access lets member-account root credentials be removed centrally so member accounts run without root credentials (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/secure-root-user-access-for-member-accounts-in-aws-organizations/)

With centralized root access, privileged tasks run as task-scoped root sessions of up to 15 minutes through `sts:AssumeRoot` from the management or delegated administrator account (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/secure-root-user-access-for-member-accounts-in-aws-organizations/)

AWS authorization combines identity-based IAM policies and resource-based policies, capped by Organizations SCPs (principal-centric) and RCPs (resource-centric), with ABAC through tags and condition keys; an explicit deny always wins (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/iam-policy-types-how-and-when-to-use-them/ ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-security-best-practices.html)
RCPs are resource-centric AWS Organizations policies that, with principal-centric SCPs, cap IAM permissions (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/iam-policy-types-how-and-when-to-use-them/)
SCPs are principal-centric AWS Organizations policies that cap identity-based and resource-based IAM permissions (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/iam-policy-types-how-and-when-to-use-them/)

The AgentCore Runtime execution role trust policy allows `bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com` to call `sts:AssumeRole` with `aws:SourceAccount` = your account and `aws:SourceArn` like `arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:<region>:<account>:*`, for confused-deputy protection (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)
Running an agent on AgentCore Runtime requires an execution role that trusts `bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

The documented AgentCore Runtime execution role permissions cover six areas: `ecr:BatchGetImage` and `ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer` on the repository plus `ecr:GetAuthorizationToken`; CloudWatch Logs actions on `/aws/bedrock-agentcore/runtimes/*`; `xray:PutTraceSegments`, `xray:PutTelemetryRecords`, `xray:GetSamplingRules` and `xray:GetSamplingTargets`; `cloudwatch:PutMetricData` limited to the `bedrock-agentcore` namespace; `bedrock-agentcore:GetWorkloadAccessToken*` on `workload-identity-directory/default/workload-identity/<agentName>-*`; and `bedrock:InvokeModel` and `bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

Direct code deployment agents use a smaller execution role: the same as the container role without the ECR statements (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

`BedrockAgentCoreFullAccess` is the broad AWS managed policy for building on AgentCore and includes `GetWorkloadAccessTokenForUserId`, which issues tokens for arbitrary user ID strings without IdP verification (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

For production, AWS advises copying only the needed statements from `BedrockAgentCoreFullAccess`, explicitly denying `GetWorkloadAccessTokenForUserId`, and granting `GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

AWS advises granting `GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT` and denying `GetWorkloadAccessTokenForUserId` for production AgentCore agents (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

IP-based conditions on Bedrock fail through VPC endpoints: `aws:SourceIp` isn't present when a request goes through a VPC endpoint, and network context is redacted when an AWS service calls Bedrock for you, so `IpAddress` conditions can't be met in those paths (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)

The `bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier` condition key (added March 2025) works on `InvokeModel`, `InvokeModelWithResponseStream`, `Converse` and `ConverseStream`; an SCP with `Null` `bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier` = `true` denies calls that have no guardrail (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-permissions-id.html ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/implementing-least-privilege-access-for-amazon-bedrock/)

A specific Bedrock guardrail can be required by IAM or SCP through the `bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier` condition key (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-permissions-id.html)

A management-account Amazon Bedrock policy in AWS Organizations applies a guardrail to every model call in OUs or accounts, and an account-level default guardrail is also supported; when an application guardrail also applies, the union applies and the most restrictive control wins (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-enforcements.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/bedrock/latest/console/hp-guardrails-org-level-management.html)

Org-level enforcement of a Standard-tier guardrail needs resource-based policies: both the guardrail and its guardrail profile (one per destination Region) must allow the organization, or calls fail with "The provided resource ARN is from a different account" (https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/bedrock-troubleshoot-guardrail-error)
AgentCore Policy supports Bedrock Guardrails (July 2026) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

Bedrock model invocation logging is off by default; when turned on, it writes full requests, responses and metadata to CloudWatch Logs or S3 in the same account and Region for `Converse`, `ConverseStream`, `InvokeModel` and `InvokeModelWithResponseStream` on `bedrock-runtime` only, and calls through `bedrock-mantle` aren't captured (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html)

In CloudTrail, Bedrock `InvokeModel`, `Converse` and their streaming variants are management events, while `InvokeAgent` (`AWS::Bedrock::AgentAlias`), `Retrieve` and `RetrieveAndGenerate` (`AWS::Bedrock::KnowledgeBase`), `InvokeFlow` and `ApplyGuardrail` are data events that need advanced event selectors (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html)
